lead: The lookout is the boat's eyes and ears. You do not need every rule of the road: your job is to see other vessels early, tell the skipper where they are and what they are doing, and recognise the few situations and signals that matter most.

qa.q: Where should I be looking when I'm on lookout on a sailing yacht?
qa.a: All round the horizon, not just ahead: a **lookout** turns to check astern every few minutes for fast ferries and RIBs, and ducks to look under the genoa, which hides the leeward bow.

blocks.p: A lookout watches **all round the horizon**, with eyes and ears, not just ahead. Fast ferries and RIBs come up from astern quickly and quietly, so turn and look behind you every few minutes.

fig.note: Starboard tack: the genoa hides the port bow

blocks.p: Under sail the genoa hides a whole sector on the **leeward bow**: on starboard tack that is the port bow. Duck down and look under the sail often.
At night your eyes need about 20 minutes of darkness to see well, and one bright white light undoes it. Read the chart by a **dim red light**.

qa.q: How do I tell the skipper where another boat is?
qa.a: Use the **clock**, counted from your own bow: 12 o'clock is dead ahead, 3 abeam to starboard, 6 astern, 9 abeam to port. Add the distance and what it is doing: "Motor boat at ten o'clock, about a mile, coming closer."

blocks.p: Report what you see, and report it early: a vessel, a buoy, a fishing float, something in the water. The skipper needs time to decide, and would rather hear of ten things that do not matter than miss one. Say **what** it is, **where** and **how far**.

fig.note: Clock bearings, counted from your own bow

blocks.p: The simplest way to say where is the **clock**, counted from your own bow: 12 o'clock is dead ahead, 3 is abeam to starboard, 6 is astern, 9 is abeam to port. Add your guess at the distance and what the vessel is doing.

blocks.rule: "Motor boat at ten o'clock, about a mile, coming closer."
blocks.label: Say

qa.q: How can I tell if another ship is on a collision course with us?
qa.a: Watch its **bearing**, several times a few minutes apart. If it stays the same while the vessel gets closer, there is risk of collision: call the skipper now. If it changes clearly, it should pass clear.

blocks.p: To tell whether another vessel will hit you or pass clear, watch its **bearing**: the compass direction to it. Take it with the hand-bearing compass, or line the vessel up with a stanchion while your boat holds a steady course. Check it several times, a few minutes apart.

fig.note: Bearing steady, ship closer each time

head: The bearing
What you report
rows: Stays the same while the vessel gets closer
Risk of collision: call the skipper now
It should pass clear. Keep checking until it is past

blocks.rule: Steady bearing, closing range: collision course.

qa.q: Does a motor boat always have to give way to a sailing yacht?
qa.a: Normally, not always: a sailing yacht keeps clear of a vessel **engaged in fishing** and of a ship that can only use a narrow channel. And when overtaking, the vessel coming up from astern keeps clear, sail or power.

blocks.p: The skipper decides what to do, but you report better when you know what should happen. One vessel **keeps clear**; the other holds her course and speed.

tiles.name: Overtaking
tiles.note: you catch up: you keep clear

blocks.p: **Overtaking**: the vessel coming up from astern keeps clear, sail or power, on any tack. **Head-on under power**: both turn to starboard and pass port to port. **Power and sail**: a vessel under power normally keeps out of the way of one under sail.

Normally, not always. A sailing yacht keeps clear of a vessel **engaged in fishing**: trawling, or with nets or long lines out that stop her turning. By day she shows two cones, points together. A boat trolling a line, or anglers with rods, get no priority. And in a **narrow channel** or harbour entrance a yacht must not get in the way of a ship that can only use that channel. A ferry leaving port will not move over for you.

qa.q: What does it mean if I see a red and a green light together at night?
qa.a: The vessel is heading straight at you: red is her port **sidelight**, green her starboard one, and seeing both means her bow points at you. Report it to the skipper at once.

blocks.p: At night you see lights, not hulls. A vessel under way shows a **red** sidelight on her port side, a **green** one to starboard and a white **sternlight** aft. Under power she adds a white **masthead light** above them; a big ship, 50 m or more, shows two, the forward one lower.

tiles.name: White over red
tiles.note: under power, crossing right to left

tiles.name: Two white and a red
tiles.note: big ship, crossing right to left

tiles.name: One white, low
tiles.note: a stern: you are behind her

blocks.p: Read the colour first. Red is her port side, so her bow points to your left; green is her starboard side, bow to your right. **Red and green together**: she is heading straight at you, so report it at once. A single white light is a stern. Sidelights with no white above them mean sail; a yacht may carry them in one **tricolour** lantern at the masthead.

qa.q: What do five short blasts on a ship's horn mean?
qa.a: A warning: five or more short, rapid blasts mean **I doubt your intentions**. The other vessel does not understand what you are doing, or thinks you are not doing enough to keep clear; tell the skipper at once.

blocks.p: Vessels under power in sight of each other announce their manoeuvres on the horn. A **short blast** lasts about a second.

head: You hear
It means
rows: I am altering my course to starboard
I am altering my course to port
Five or more short, rapid blasts
I doubt your intentions: a warning

blocks.p: Five short blasts aimed at your boat mean the other vessel does not understand what you are doing, or thinks you are not doing enough to keep clear. Tell the skipper at once.
